question.problem: Given that $p(x)=6{x}^{9}$ and $q(x)=15{x}^{7},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)}{p(x)}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's calculate ${x}^{2}\cdot q(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)={x}^{2}\cdot (15{x}^{7})=15{x}^{9}
$$

When we divide the two functions ${x}^{2}\cdot q(x)$ and $p(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)}{p(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{15{x}^{9}}{6{x}^{9}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{15}{6} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
